book.title: In Search of Lost Time
book.author: Marcel Proust
book.description: Explore Proust’s seven volumes, from the models of Combray and Balbec to Paris, Venice and Padua.
book.help: Choose a volume to explore its places.
book.sidebarNote: Real places, fictional settings and documented models. Each record explains what its marker can locate.
book.footerHtml:
Seven volumes, with real settings and documented models distinguished in every record. Streets and areas have representative markers; fictional houses, railway stations and private interiors without a verified position remain unlocated.

Proust · original volumes

Download location records (CSV)

chapters.title: Swann’s Way
chapters.text: The remembered house and childhood walks lead to Swann’s love for Odette and the narrator’s meetings with Gilberte in Paris. The map separates real streets from the models of fictional Combray.
placeText: Combray · memory and childhood; real model in Illiers
Saint-Hilaire dominates Combray’s remembered townscape. Saint-Jacques is shown as one documented inspiration.
Swann’s park and Gilberte belong to the childhood walks; the real garden is shown as a model.
Swann’s earlier Paris home is on quai d’Orléans. The house number is not established.
Swann accompanies Odette to her home on rue La Pérouse. The marker identifies the street.
The Verdurins’ earlier salon is on rue Montalivet, an address recalled explicitly in The Prisoner.
The narrator hopes to meet Gilberte in the gardens and shares her games.
With Françoise, the narrator goes to the bridge to look at the frozen Seine.
Odette’s promenades and the closing return to the Bois connect desire with the loss of the past.
chapters.note: The map shows documented real places and models. Combray, Balbec, Doncières and the Raspelière are fictional constructions. No continuous route or exact private address is inferred where the evidence does not support it.

chapters.title: In the Shadow of Young Girls in Flower
chapters.text: Parisian affection and artistic expectations give way to the first stay at Balbec. The hotel, the sea and the group of young girls reshape the narrator’s sense of beauty.
placeText: Games, affection and disappointment continue the narrator’s relationship with Gilberte.
The Balbec hotel frames the stay by the sea and the narrator’s encounters. Cabourg is its documented model.
The young girls and Albertine appear on Balbec’s seafront. The Cabourg promenade is shown as a model, without an exact encounter point.
chapters.note: The map shows documented real places and models. Combray, Balbec, Doncières and the Raspelière are fictional constructions. No continuous route or exact private address is inferred where the evidence does not support it.

chapters.title: The Guermantes Way
chapters.text: The fascination with aristocratic society grows around the Guermantes home and the theatre. The grandmother’s illness turns familiar Paris into the setting of loss. Doncières has no single verified real-world position in this atlas.
placeText: The family’s apartment and the Guermantes household are fictional private interiors; the street is only an orientation reference.
The theatre and the Opéra offer a view of the Guermantes world as well as artistic experience.
An outing with his grandmother precedes her grave illness; Carnavalet identifies the gardens as this episode’s setting.
chapters.note: The map shows documented real places and models. Combray, Balbec, Doncières and the Raspelière are fictional constructions. No continuous route or exact private address is inferred where the evidence does not support it.

chapters.title: Sodom and Gomorrah
chapters.text: The discovery of concealed relationships is followed by a second stay at Balbec, memories of the grandmother and visits to the Verdurins. The little railway and its fictional stations are described but are not forced onto an unverified modern route.
placeText: The family’s apartment and the Guermantes household are fictional private interiors; the street is only an orientation reference.
The second Balbec stay awakens the painful memory of the grandmother.
The young girls and Albertine appear on Balbec’s seafront. The Cabourg promenade is shown as a model, without an exact encounter point.

chapters.title: The Prisoner
chapters.setting: Paris · apartment, Bois and Verdurin salon
chapters.text: Life with Albertine centres on a Paris apartment, jealousy and restricted freedom. The outings and the musical evening at the Verdurins provide identifiable public references around fictional interiors.
placeText: The family’s apartment and the Guermantes household are fictional private interiors; the street is only an orientation reference.
Rare outings with Albertine interrupt her confinement in the apartment.
The narrator stops his carriage and joins Brichot near the quay end of rue Bonaparte.
The Verdurin salon hosts the musical evening organised by Charlus and the break with Morel.
chapters.note: The map shows documented real places and models. Combray, Balbec, Doncières and the Raspelière are fictional constructions. No continuous route or exact private address is inferred where the evidence does not support it.

chapters.title: The Fugitive · Albertine Gone
chapters.text: Grief and the gradual transformation of memory lead from Paris to Venice with the narrator’s mother. The Venetian streets, art and a clearly narrated visit to Giotto’s chapel in Padua expand this volume’s geography.
placeText: The narrator returns to the Bois after Albertine’s death, revisiting the landscape of their outings.
The campanile seen from the lodging and the nearby Piazzetta shape the mornings in Venice; the marker locates the basilica complex.
The narrator meets his mother on the Piazzetta, then they go up the Grand Canal in a gondola.
Carpaccio’s paintings unexpectedly revive a painful memory of Albertine.
Before leaving Venice, the narrator goes to Padua and enters Giotto’s chapel after crossing the Arena garden.

chapters.title: Time Regained
chapters.text: Tansonville and the transformed Paris of the war lead to the final reception and the discovery of a literary vocation. The uneven paving recalls Venice, but the reception’s fictional courtyard is not given an invented precise address.
placeText: The stay with Gilberte revisits Tansonville and changes the narrator’s understanding of the two childhood ways. The marker remains the documented garden model.
The old Trocadéro towers appear against the sunset during the wartime walk.
From the Pont des Invalides the narrator wanders towards the Grands Boulevards.
The wartime boulevards are crowded with soldiers and the altered nightlife of Paris. This is a district reference, not an exact stop.
The later encounter with the diminished Charlus returns the reader to the Champs-Élysées.
The final reception belongs to the new Princess de Guermantes’s residence on avenue du Bois. The courtyard itself remains unmapped.

leonie.name: Aunt Léonie’s house · Amiot house
leonie.note: The Amiot family house is the documented model for the aunt’s house in Combray. The historical street address locates the house; the museum now welcomes visitors at 4 place Lemoine. Combray is a literary reconstruction.
leonie.method: Official BAN address point returned by IGN. This identifies the postal address, not an interior room or a surveyed entrance. Decimal digits do not express a measured error margin.

church.note: Saint-Jacques is a documented inspiration for Saint-Hilaire. Proust combines architectural memories; the fictional church is not a literal description of this building.
church.method: IGN BD TOPO named-place record. The coordinate is a representative point of the feature, not an entrance or the exact position of a character.

garden.name: Tansonville park · model: Pré Catelan
garden.note: The garden created by Jules Amiot inspired Swann’s park. This marker locates the real garden, not a verified position of Swann’s fictional house or its hawthorn hedge.
garden.method: Coordinate published by Eure-et-Loir Tourisme on Cirkwi, reproduced unchanged. It is the garden’s tourist point, not a surveyed scene location.
